_about.one_line: Six OpenCode plugins and four CLI tools that cut what coding agents send to paid models, with a pre-registered paired A/B.
_about.source: README.md, DOSSIER.md, Makefile, release-scan.txt, tests/*, ab/* (pre-registration, tasks, runs, result, RESULT.md)

tests.title: Six OpenCode plugins: 6 test files pass (36 assertions)
tests.claim: 'make test: 6 plugin test files (node:test, 36 assertions) + the token-baseline test, all pass' (DOSSIER). The plugins are minimal-system, context-gate, output-compact, context-trim, cloud-pacer and sanitize-cloud-payload.
tests.verify: N=node; v=$(node -p "process.versions.node.split('.').slice(0,2).map(Number).reduce((a,b)=>a*1000+b)" 2>/dev/null || echo 0); [ "$v" -ge 22006 ] || for c in "$HOME"/.nvm/versions/node/v2[2-9]*/bin/node /usr/local/bin/node; do [ -x "$c" ] && [ "$($c -p "process.versions.node.split('.').slice(0,2).map(Number).reduce((a,b)=>a*1000+b)")" -ge 22006 ] && N=$c && break; done; $N --experimental-strip-types --test tests/test_*.mjs 2>&1 | grep -E "^# (tests|pass|fail)" | tee /tmp/cs1.$$; grep -q "^# pass 6" /tmp/cs1.$$ && grep -q "^# fail 0" /tmp/cs1.$$; r=$?; rm -f /tmp/cs1.$$; exit $r
tests.what_it_means: Each plugin loads and its hooks behave on a sample: minimal-system replaces a verbose system prompt with one under 1000 characters containing 'Be direct and tool-driven'; output-compact collapses blank lines, truncates at 16,000 characters and names a grep hint for huge listings; context-trim caps history at 50 messages and each text part at 5,500 characters; context-gate redirects broad early file reads; cloud-pacer returns at once for local models and survives a rate-limit event; sanitize-cloud-payload strips an AWS key, a private-key header, DB artifact names and brand patterns. Passing shows the hooks work as coded. It does not show they save money in real use: that is the A/B (CS3 to CS6).
tests.how_we_got_it: tests/test_*.mjs (node:test), run with `node --experimental-strip-types --test tests/test_*.mjs` on Node v22.23.2 on this laptop on 2026-10-16: tests 6, pass 6, fail 0. The tests copy the .ts plugin to a temp file in /tmp and import it (the copy rewrites one import to `import type`). The assertion count of 36 was counted by grep over the six files: 4+6+5+6+8+7.
tests.use_in_your_work: Drop any one of the six plugins into your own OpenCode setup and run its test first: it shows exactly what the plugin changes in the prompt or the tool output.
tests.honest_limits: Needs Node 22.6 or newer: on Node 18.19.1 (the default on this laptop) the command fails with 'node: bad option: --experimental-strip-types'. The Makefile does not say this. The tests exercise hook behaviour with stubs, not a live OpenCode.

tests.title: Token-baseline tool test (fixture only)
tests.claim: The token-baseline test passes (DOSSIER: 'the token-baseline test, all pass').
tests.verify: T=$(mktemp -d); cp -a . "$T/r"; (cd "$T/r"; export PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1; python3 tests/test_fleet_token_baseline.py) > "$T/o" 2>&1; rc=$?; tail -n 3 "$T/o"; grep -Eq 'fleet-token-baseline test passed' "$T/o" && [ $rc -eq 0 ]; r=$?; rm -rf "$T"; exit $r
tests.what_it_means: The test builds a one-row fake opencode.db and a fake dispatch.db and checks the row reads back with total 1500 tokens. Honestly, it asserts on the fixture it just wrote; it does not invoke bin/fleet-token-baseline. It proves SQLite fixtures can be built, not that the report tool is correct.
tests.how_we_got_it: tests/test_fleet_token_baseline.py, run with python3 on this laptop on 2026-10-16 in a temp copy: prints '[+] fleet-token-baseline test passed'. pytest also collects it: 1 passed.
tests.use_in_your_work: Do not rely on it as a gate for the report tool; if you adopt the tool, add a test that runs it against a fixture database and compares the printed totals.
tests.honest_limits: Weak coverage: the tool under test is never executed by this test.

tests.title: Pre-registered A/B verdict: PASS (median -89.3% fresh tokens, p = 0.0046, 16/16 vs 15/16)
tests.claim: 'Pre-registered verdict PASS (median -89.3% fresh tokens in+out, p = 0.0046, success 16/16 vs 15/16)' on 16 paired tasks.
tests.verify:
python3 - <<'PY'
import json
s=json.load(open('ab/cost-savers-AB-v2.result.json'))['summary']
assert s['n_pairs']==16 and s['PASS'] is True
assert abs(s['median_reduction_P']-0.8934611)<1e-6 and abs(s['wilcoxon_p']-0.0045929)<1e-6
assert s['success_A']==0.9375 and s['success_B']==1.0
print('PASS n=16 median_reduction_P=%.1f%% p=%.4f success A 15/16 B 16/16'%(s['median_reduction_P']*100,s['wilcoxon_p']))
PY
tests.expect: PASS n=16 median_reduction_P=89.3% p=0.0046 success A 15/16 B 16/16
tests.what_it_means: Across 16 short read-only questions, the arm with the six plugins used a median 89.3% fewer fresh tokens (input plus output) than the arm without, one-sided Wilcoxon p = 0.0046, and answered 16 of 16 correctly against 15 of 16. All three pre-registered criteria are met (20% reduction, p < 0.05, success within 5 points). The read-out is only the pre-registered metric; CS4 and CS5 hold the declared secondaries that qualify it.
tests.how_we_got_it: Pre-registration cost-savers-AB-PREREG-v2.md (2026-10-01, written before any run); frozen tasks ab/ab_v2_tasks.json; harness ab/run_ab_v2.py (32 runs shuffled with seed 20260929, opencode 1.18.33, model opencode/space-bunny-free, token counts read back from opencode's session database); analysis ab/analyze_ab_v2.py (needs scipy and the author's opencode.db) writes ab/cost-savers-AB-v2.result.json. This check re-reads that committed result file. CS6 recomputes the headline numbers from the run records.
tests.use_in_your_work: Use it as a template for how to test a cost tool honestly: write the tasks and the pass bar first, pair the runs, and publish the verdict whichever way it falls.
tests.honest_limits: Short read-only sessions on one free model; long sessions and other providers are untested (DOSSIER Limits).

tests.title: Negative qualifier: processed tokens including cache reads barely changed (-2.2%)
tests.claim: 'All processed tokens incl. cache reads: 1,309,670 vs 1,280,506, -2.2% (median -0.07%)'; the fresh-token saving comes from provider prompt-cache hits, cause not isolated (RESULT.md, README, DOSSIER).
tests.verify:
python3 - <<'PY'
import json
s=json.load(open('ab/cost-savers-AB-v2.result.json'))['summary']
assert s['sum_total_A']==1309670 and s['sum_total_B']==1280506
ch=s['sum_total_B']/s['sum_total_A']-1
assert abs(ch+0.0223)<0.0001 and abs(s['median_reduction_total_incl_cache']+0.00073)<0.00001
print('total incl cache: %d -> %d (%.1f%%), median %.2f%%'%(s['sum_total_A'],s['sum_total_B'],ch*100,s['median_reduction_total_incl_cache']*100*-1*-1))
PY
tests.what_it_means: Adding the tokens served from the provider's cache, both arms processed about the same amount of context: 1,309,670 without the plugins, 1,280,506 with them, a 2.2% sum reduction and 0.07% median. So the 89.3% headline is a saving in fresh (non-cached) tokens, which providers usually bill at a higher rate than cache reads; it is not a smaller context. RESULT.md says the plugins may keep the prompt prefix stable, or run order may have warmed the cache, and the design cannot tell which.
tests.how_we_got_it: Same result file as CS3 (the secondary fields sum_total_A, sum_total_B and median_reduction_total_incl_cache), computed by ab/analyze_ab_v2.py from cache-read counts in opencode's session table. RESULT.md adds a billing illustration, explicitly not a measurement: at a cache-read price of 10% of fresh input, billed tokens would be A about 486,000 vs B about 284,000 (about -42%).
tests.use_in_your_work: Before you quote a token saving, ask which tokens: fresh, cached or total. Your bill depends on the price of each.
tests.honest_limits: A negative-leaning result kept on purpose. A randomised-cache long-session A/B is listed in the DOSSIER as the planned next measurement; it has not been run.

tests.title: Negative qualifier: the plugin arm was slower (median 31.2 s vs 12.0 s)
tests.claim: 'Median wall time per task: 12.0 s without, 31.2 s with the plugins - B slower' (RESULT.md, README: 'slower (pacing)').
tests.verify:
python3 - <<'PY'
import json
s=json.load(open('ab/cost-savers-AB-v2.result.json'))['summary']
assert s['median_wall_A']==12.0 and s['median_wall_B']==31.15
print('median wall A %.1f s, B %.1f s'%(s['median_wall_A'],s['median_wall_B']))
PY
tests.expect: median wall A 12.0 s, B 31.1 s
tests.what_it_means: With the plugins on, a typical task took 31.15 s against 12.0 s. The RESULT.md reads this as consistent with cloud-pacer, which deliberately delays requests; the DOSSIER says 'cloud-pacer deliberately slows requests'. The A/B does not separate pacing from the other plugins' effects, so the cause is the authors' reading, not a measured attribution.
tests.how_we_got_it: From the same 32 recorded runs (wall_s per run in ab/cost-savers-AB-v2.runs.jsonl), medians computed by ab/analyze_ab_v2.py into the result file. The README rounds 31.15 to 31.2.
tests.use_in_your_work: If you use the pacer for free-tier or rate-limited providers, expect a latency cost; leave it out for local models.
tests.honest_limits: Latency here was measured on a free model with provider-side variance; no repeat of the timing is recorded.

tests.title: Independent recomputation of the A/B headline from the 32 run records (stdlib only)
tests.claim: The headline numbers (sums 394,512 and 173,138; median reduction 89.3%; one-sided Wilcoxon p = 0.0046; success 15/16 and 16/16) follow from the committed per-run records, not only from the committed summary.
tests.verify:
python3 - <<'PY'
import json, statistics
runs=[json.loads(l) for l in open('ab/cost-savers-AB-v2.runs.jsonl')]
by={}
for r in runs: by.setdefault(r['task'],{})[r['arm']]=r
pairs=[(d['A'],d['B']) for t,d in sorted(by.items()) if 'A' in d and 'B' in d and d['A'].get('tokens_in') is not None and d['B'].get('tokens_in') is not None]
P=lambda r:r['tokens_in']+r['tokens_out']
sa=sum(P(a) for a,b in pairs); sb=sum(P(b) for a,b in pairs)
med=statistics.median((P(a)-P(b))/P(a) for a,b in pairs)
nz=[P(a)-P(b) for a,b in pairs if P(a)!=P(b)]
order=sorted(range(len(nz)),key=lambda i:abs(nz[i]))
rk=[0]*len(nz); i=0
while i<len(order):
    j=i
    while j+1<len(order) and abs(nz[order[j+1]])==abs(nz[order[i]]): j+=1
    for k in range(i,j+1): rk[order[k]]=(i+j)/2+1
    i=j+1
wp=sum(r for r,d in zip(rk,nz) if d>0)
cnt=sum(1 for m in range(2**len(nz)) if sum(rk[k] for k in range(len(nz)) if m>>k&1)>=wp-1e-9)
p=cnt/2**len(nz)
sA=sum(a['success'] for a,b in pairs); sB=sum(b['success'] for a,b in pairs)
assert (len(pairs),sa,sb,sA,sB)==(16,394512,173138,15,16) and abs(med-0.8934611)<1e-6 and abs(p-0.0046)<0.0001
print('recomputed: n=%d sumP %d -> %d, median reduction %.1f%%, exact one-sided Wilcoxon p=%.4f, success %d/16 vs %d/16'%(len(pairs),sa,sb,med*100,p,sA,sB))
PY
tests.expect: recomputed: n=16 sumP 394512 -> 173138, median reduction 89.3%, exact one-sided Wilcoxon p=0.0046, success 15/16 vs 16/16
tests.what_it_means: Starting from the 32 raw run records (arm, tokens in/out, success), pairing by task and computing the pre-registered statistic reproduces the sums, the 89.3% median reduction and the one-sided Wilcoxon p-value (here as an exact enumeration of the signed-rank sums, without scipy; it matches scipy's 0.0046 to four places). So the verdict does not depend on trusting the summary file. It still depends on the run records being what the harness wrote; the token counts themselves came from opencode's session database on the author's machine, which is not in the repo.
tests.how_we_got_it: Pure python3 over ab/cost-savers-AB-v2.runs.jsonl (32 lines, 16 tasks x 2 arms). The authors' analysis script is ab/analyze_ab_v2.py (scipy.stats.wilcoxon and the opencode.db for cache reads); this check replaces both with stdlib arithmetic and does not need the database. Written for this suite record on 2026-10-16.
tests.use_in_your_work: A model of an auditable result: keep every raw run, and let a reader recompute the headline in a few seconds.
tests.honest_limits: Re-derives the statistic only; cannot re-check that tokens were counted correctly at run time or re-run the agent.

tests.title: A/B integrity: 16 frozen tasks, 32 runs, fixed shuffle seed, pre-registered before the runs
tests.claim: Pre-registration written before any run; 16 frozen read-only questions; 32 runs shuffled with seed 20260929 (ab/README.md).
tests.verify:
python3 - <<'PY'
import json
t=json.load(open('ab/ab_v2_tasks.json'))
runs=[l for l in open('ab/cost-savers-AB-v2.runs.jsonl') if l.strip()]
assert len(t)==16 and all('expect' in x and 'prompt' in x for x in t) and len(runs)==32
assert '20260929' in open('ab/run_ab_v2.py').read()
assert 'written BEFORE any run' in open('ab/cost-savers-AB-PREREG-v2.md').read()
print('16 tasks, 32 runs, seed 20260929, prereg says written BEFORE any run')
PY
tests.expect: 16 tasks, 32 runs, seed 20260929, prereg says written BEFORE any run
tests.what_it_means: The files that make the experiment checkable are all there and agree on size: 16 questions with expected answers, 32 recorded runs, a harness with the shuffle seed, and a pre-registration that states it was written before any run. This shows the design was fixed in advance on paper; it cannot prove the timing of the pre-registration, which rests on the committed text and the git history.
tests.how_we_got_it: ab/README.md lists the files; reproduction needs the author's opencode config, a clone of the Omnitool repo at /tmp/ab/repo and a working opencode with the free model (not re-run here; billable-free but network-bound).
tests.use_in_your_work: Copy the structure for your own A/B: tasks, expected answers, seed, pass bar, runs.
tests.honest_limits: Re-running the A/B needs OpenCode, network and the same free model; the model may no longer be offered.

tests.title: Withdrawn earlier figures stay withdrawn (simulated Arm B on 09-29)
tests.claim: 'An A/B result was produced by a script that simulated Arm B; caught on 10-01 and withdrawn'; the earlier figures (1,893,904,352 characters saved, 64.1%, p < 0.001, ...) 'appear in no data file, script or log in the repository' (DOSSIER, RESULT.md).
tests.verify: grep -q 'simulated Arm B' DOSSIER.md && grep -q 'Earlier figures withdrawn' ab/cost-savers-AB-v2-RESULT.md && grep -q 'are withdrawn' ab/cost-savers-AB-v2-RESULT.md && n=$(grep -rIl --exclude-dir=.git --exclude=cost-savers-AB-v2-RESULT.md -e '1,893,904,352' -e '64.1%' . | wc -l) && [ "$n" -eq 0 ] && echo 'withdrawn figures appear only in the withdrawal note'
tests.expect: withdrawn figures appear only in the withdrawal note
tests.what_it_means: The earlier 64.1% / 1.89-billion-character claim is not in the repo as a result; it is named once, in the RESULT.md withdrawal note, as untraceable and withdrawn, and the pre-registration records that the 09-29 result came from a script that simulated the treatment arm. The check confirms no other file still carries those numbers. It does not confirm that nobody quoted them elsewhere before the withdrawal.
tests.how_we_got_it: DOSSIER creation-history rows 09-29 and 10-01, the pre-registration's 'Supersedes' paragraph and RESULT.md's last section; the grep is run over the whole clone.
tests.use_in_your_work: A reminder to withdraw a bad number in public, in writing, with a reason.
tests.honest_limits: The withdrawn script (run_ab_eval.py) is not shipped, so the simulation itself cannot be inspected here.

tests.title: Release scan: no leaks, no development paths, nothing vendored

tests.verify: grep -q 'no leaks found' release-scan.txt && grep -q 'machine (grep -rn over the tree): 0' release-scan.txt && ! grep -rIl --exclude-dir=.git --exclude=release-scan.txt -E '/home/[a-z]+/' . && echo 'scan recorded; no /home/<user>/ path in the tree'
tests.expect: scan recorded; no /home/<user>/ path in the tree
tests.what_it_means: The committed scan reports no secrets and no developer paths, and the path grep is re-run on the clone. gitleaks itself is not re-run.
tests.how_we_got_it: release-scan.txt (gitleaks 8.24.0, `detect --no-git -s . --redact`; its make-test line is dated 2026-09-29).
tests.use_in_your_work: Run both checks on your own plugin repo before you publish.
